newsitem.title: FRANCE: MATIF report outlines EMU battle plan.
newsitem.headline: MATIF report outlines EMU battle plan.

text.p: French futures and options exchange MATIF outlined its battle plan on Wednesday for retaining a healthy slice of the futures market after the planned introduction of single European currency in 1999.

A report by a MATIF working committee recommended the launch of a euro-interest rate future, a five-year bond future and explored the practical difficulties in switching existing contracts into euro-denominated products.

Jacques Werren, MATIF deputy managing director, said at a news conference he recognised that rival London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) had the upper hand in some areas, especially interest rate futures.

But he said all that could change in 1999, which he likened to a Europe-wide "Big Bang", and that MATIF was in a position to benefit substantially from the changeover especially if a European money market developed alongside the London market.

"The European Monetary Union (EMU) zone will become MATIF's domestic market base, an advantage to be exploited particularly at the short end of the yield curve so that the Euro money market differentiates itself clearly from the London market," he said in the report.

The working committee urged the establishment of new benchmark short-term interest rates set up by a panel of 20 to 30 banks within the European single currency zone. This would create a "Euribor", or average inter-bank rate offered by EU banks to prime borrowers.

"Should the United Kingdom not join EMU, or should obligatory reserves be imposed on banks inside the EMU zone, the European money market could be divided between a continental and an offshore market, which would justify the existence of two distinct benchmarks," the report said.

The ailing Ecu market received little comfort from the report. France is one of the few countries still trying to support the Ecu bond market, but the working group said it rejected the idea of launching any more Ecu derivative products.

"The members of the working committee have reservations about the future of the Ecu between now and 1999, and reject a priori a strategy based on developing a range of Ecu products on MATIF ahead of the transition to the euro," the report said.
At a conference organised by MATIF on Wednesday to discuss the move to a single currency, Gerard Pfauwadel, MATIF chairman, was in an upbeat mood.
"We are the only ones to be able to show today a coherent strategy for the switch to the euro," he said.
